summary: Cap-de-Bon-Désir light on Quebec's north shore: a steel tower lit in 1941, the octagonal concrete tower of 1958, automated by 1982, still in service.

light.fog_signal: type F diaphone with five-second blasts every forty seconds (1958 to 1971); electric foghorn from 1971, deactivated 1997

lens.type: DCB-10 dioptric apparatus with two ten-inch Fresnel lenses

light.focal_plane_note: LighthouseFriends gives a focal plane of 146 feet (44.5 m); the Coast Guard list gives 46.4 m.

structures.type: steel skeleton tower with acetylene lamp
structures.note: First light. LighthouseFriends places it near the shore where the information centre now stands.

structures.type: octagonal reinforced-concrete tower with red top
structures.note: Present tower; the Coast Guard list gives 14.3 m for it.
Houses the diaphone, later the compressors and tanks; the Quebec record gives the 1958 buildings as the station's second phase.

access.note: Paid entry for adults at the interpretation centre (Parks Canada); tower closed.

visit.note: Interpretation centre in the former head keeper's house, with displays on lighthouses and marine life (LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: Canadian Coast Guard (the light); Parks Canada manages the site within the Saguenay–St. Lawrence Marine Park

events.note: First light: steel skeleton tower with acetylene lamp, built after a Pilots Corporation petition.
Contract for the present tower awarded to Euclide Tremblay and Camille Dufour (LighthouseFriends).
Present octagonal reinforced-concrete tower, fog-signal building and two residences completed; cost $53,749.
DCB-10 dioptric apparatus; station operational 10 October 1958.
Type F diaphone in the fog-signal building.
Automation begins (Quebec record); LighthouseFriends dates the first equipment to 1972.
Electric foghorn replaces the diaphone; four-second blast each minute.

corrections.why: The Quebec record dates the present tower 1958 (Construction) and says it came into operation in 1958; LighthouseFriends says the contract was let in 1957 and the work finished the following year. 1957 is the contract year.
The OpenStreetMap-derived height does not match the Quebec record, LighthouseFriends or Routes des phares (10.7 m). The Coast Guard list gives 14.3 m, which is not reconciled; see notes_for_editor.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The station record's 1957 (from the Lighthouse Directory) is the contract year (LighthouseFriends). The Quebec record and LighthouseFriends agree the tower came into service in 1958.
The Quebec record gives 1971 as the start of automation; LighthouseFriends dates the first equipment to 1972. Both are shown in the story.

notes_for_editor: 1) Height: 10.7 m (Quebec record, LighthouseFriends, Routes des phares) against 14.3 m (Coast Guard list, which may measure something else). The story gives 10.7 m and says what the Coast Guard list says. 2) Focal height: the Coast Guard list gives 46.4 m (152 ft); LighthouseFriends gives a focal plane of 146 feet (44.5 m). Not reconciled. 3) Automation start 1971 (Quebec) against 1972 (LighthouseFriends). 4) The keeper roster rests on LighthouseFriends alone. Esdras Beaulieu, Léonid Lavoie and Lucien Dionne have no dates in any source read. Gilbert Fraser's service ended after 1960 and is named only in his public role. 5) LighthouseFriends' 1941 account of the Pilots Corporation petition and the 1957 contract has no archival check: the Department of Transport annual reports (1941 to 1958) are not in the local corpus, and LighthouseFriends cites the 1959 report without a page. 6) A Library and Archives Canada catalogue record (RG12, 1975-387, 'Cap Bon Désir - Lighthouse under construction', dated 1941) turned up in search but returned 403 and was not read, so it is not cited; it may be a usable photo, to check for licence. 7) The Wikimedia Commons photo in the station record was not checked here. 8) Staffing as of 1982 is from both the Quebec record and LighthouseFriends.
